system:
You are the Issuing authority reviewer, standing in for the national emergency authority that issues alerts (who, where, when). You check that this sender may issue this alert, for this area, now: the sender is in the issuer register, the target area is the one requested for this event, the status fits the context (a drill stays a drill), it does not overreach an active alert from a higher authority, and a correction points to the alert it corrects.
You see only the issuer register, active and earlier alerts, the requested area and the alert's status, type, sender and area. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

[FCC-HI-2018#0084] Report and Recommendations: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency January 13, 2018 False Alert (p.15):
HI-EMA’s procedures for conducting a ballistic missile drill lacked adequate safeguards that might have helped to avoid the communication errors that led to the false alert.74 First, the ballistic missile checklist lacked guidelines for HI-EMA staff for conducting an internal drill, including how to create or modify an internal drill initiation message.75 As a matter of general practice, the HI-EMA procedure for an internal drill used language identical to that contained in the checklist for actual ballistic missile alerts—including the phrase “real world”—but added the words “exercise, exercise, exercise” both before and after the message to indicate that it was a drill. Use of the same language for both test and live alert initiation procedures could cause confusion among warning officers who received the message without prior notice, notwithstanding the statements at the beginning and end of the message that it was an exercise.

[ON-PICKERING-2020#0085] Investigation into the emergency alerts sent on January 12, 2020 (Live and training systems):
Live and training systems The Alert Ready system has a training system and a live system. As the names suggest, the former is for users to practice sending alerts; the latter is for real events. The process for issuing an alert on the training system closely mimics the live system, however the training alert terminates in the system after the final prompt.

[ON-PICKERING-2020#0086] Investigation into the emergency alerts sent on January 12, 2020 (Live and training systems):
Login credentials for the live and training systems are the same. Both training and live systems can be open simultaneously on the same device. The user interface is visually similar for both systems. They are differentiated largely by font and background colour and the words ‘training’ and ‘live.’ Prompts are pushed to the user throughout the alert issuance process on both systems, with the prompts on the live system indicating that a live alert will be issued should the user continue. The prompts on the training system largely mimic those on the live system.

[ON-PICKERING-2020#0089] Investigation into the emergency alerts sent on January 12, 2020 (Findings):
The training system is similar to the live system in order to simulate issuing a real alert. The process and prompts are nearly identical with the exception of a final confirmation prompt on the live system. Despite different font and background colours, the live and training system interfaces are similar. The login credentials are the same for both training and live systems.

[ON-PICKERING-2020#0013] Investigation into the emergency alerts sent on January 12, 2020 (Key findings):
On January 12, 2020, the DO logged in to the Alert Ready live system, believed they had switched to the training system, selected a pre-scripted nuclear template for the PNGS and accidentally sent a live alert.

[CAPCP#0119] Canadian Profile of the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP-CP): Introduction and Rule Set 1.0 (Draft 2) (Recommendation #1. Preferential treatment of <polygon> and <circle>):
Example: Element: Use: Optional Type: Technical Value: Description: CAP-CP requires either a CAP-CP <geocode> value, or the use of optional <polygon> and <circle> values. When either or both <polygon> and <circle> values are present in an area block, the combination of these <polygon> and <circle> values alone is considered a more accurate representation of the alert area than the CAP supported combination of all <polygon>, <circle> and <geocode> values together. This distinction allows for CAP originators to support alerting systems that require geocodes and still be able to more accurately represent the threat area with GIS constructs all in one CAP message. E.g. Use of a location code for an entire city, with a polygon representing an alert that is specific to just a few blocks.

data.summary: This request is for a practice alert on the training system, but the console is live and the alert is set to status Actual with Public scope for a nuclear incident at Pickering. That is the 2020 Pickering false-alert pattern. A person must stop this and confirm it before anything is sent. The alert area is also undefined: no area was intended, and the areaDesc is 'unknown' with no geocode or polygon.

objections.issue: The context is an exercise and the requested area says it is a training-system practice alert. However, the console environment is live and the alert status is Actual, scope Public. Sending this would put a real public nuclear alert out from a drill, which is exactly the Pickering 2020 failure.
objections.fix: Do not send from the live console. Move to the training system and set status to Exercise. A person must confirm that no live alert is intended before any further action.
